[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Git Attributes: .gitattributes"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"The .gitattributes file is a powerful tool in Git that allows you to define attributes for paths. These attributes can influence how Git handles specific files or directories within your repository. This tutorial will guide you through the basics of using .gitattributes to customize Git's behavior."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"What is .gitattributes?"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"The .gitattributes file is a simple text file that resides within your Git repository. It uses a pattern-based syntax to associate attributes with specific files or directories. These attributes can control various aspects of Git's behavior, such as line ending normalization, diffing, merging, and more."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"Location of .gitattributes"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"A .gitattributes file can be placed in any directory within your repository. Attributes defined in a .gitattributes file apply to the directory it's located in and all its subdirectories. You can also have a global .gitattributes file that applies to all Git repositories on your system. This is configured using 'git config --global core.attributesfile'."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Syntax of .gitattributes"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"The syntax of a .gitattributes file is straightforward. Each line consists of a pattern followed by one or more attributes, separated by spaces. The pattern specifies the files or directories to which the attributes apply."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"*.txt text eol=lf
*.png binary"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"In this example, '*.txt' matches all files with the '.txt' extension, and 'text eol=lf' sets the 'text' attribute and configures line endings to use LF (Line Feed). '*.png' matches all '.png' files and marks them as binary."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"Common Attributes"},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"text: Declares whether a file is text or binary. Git treats text files differently, especially regarding line endings."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"eol: Controls line ending normalization. Common values are 'lf' (Line Feed), 'crlf' (Carriage Return Line Feed), and 'native' (use the platform's native line endings)."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"binary: Equivalent to 'text=false'. Marks a file as binary, preventing Git from attempting line ending normalization or diffing."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"diff: Specifies a custom diff driver for comparing files. This is useful for file formats that Git doesn't understand natively."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"merge: Specifies a custom merge driver for resolving conflicts in files. Similar to 'diff', this is useful for specialized file formats."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"export-ignore: Excludes files from being exported when creating archives (e.g., using 'git archive')."},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Line Ending Normalization"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"One of the most common uses of .gitattributes is to handle line ending differences between operating systems. Windows uses CRLF, while Linux and macOS use LF. Git can automatically convert line endings to ensure consistency across platforms."},{"order":20,"type":"code","text":"*.txt text eol=lf
*.sh text eol=lf
*.js text eol=lf"},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"This configuration ensures that all '.txt', '.sh', and '.js' files use LF line endings in the repository, regardless of the developer's operating system. Git will automatically convert CRLF to LF when committing and LF to CRLF when checking out on Windows."},{"order":22,"type":"subheading","text":"Binary Files"},{"order":23,"type":"paragraph","text":"For binary files, it's important to prevent Git from attempting line ending normalization or diffing, as this can corrupt the files. Use the 'binary' attribute to mark binary files."},{"order":24,"type":"code","text":"*.png binary
*.jpg binary
*.gif binary"},{"order":25,"type":"paragraph","text":"This configuration tells Git to treat '.png', '.jpg', and '.gif' files as binary files."},{"order":26,"type":"subheading","text":"Custom Diff and Merge Drivers"},{"order":27,"type":"paragraph","text":"For specialized file formats, you can define custom diff and merge drivers to improve Git's ability to compare and merge these files. This involves configuring Git to use external tools for diffing and merging."},{"order":28,"type":"code","text":"[diff "mydiff"]
	command = mydiffscript
[merge "mymerge"]
	command = mymergescript
	name = My Merge Driver"},{"order":29,"type":"code","text":"*.myext diff=mydiff merge=mymerge"},{"order":30,"type":"paragraph","text":"This example defines a custom diff driver named 'mydiff' and a custom merge driver named 'mymerge'. The 'command' specifies the script to execute for diffing and merging. The '*.myext' line associates these drivers with files having the '.myext' extension."},{"order":31,"type":"subheading","text":"Applying .gitattributes"},{"order":32,"type":"paragraph","text":"Changes to .gitattributes only affect files that are subsequently committed. To apply changes to existing files, you may need to update the index. This can be done by removing the files from the index and re-adding them."},{"order":33,"type":"code","text":"git rm --cached -r .
git add ."},{"order":34,"type":"paragraph","text":"This command removes all files from the index (without deleting them from the working directory) and then re-adds them, applying the new .gitattributes rules."},{"order":35,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":36,"type":"paragraph","text":"The .gitattributes file is a versatile tool for customizing Git's behavior on a per-file or per-directory basis. By understanding its syntax and available attributes, you can fine-tune Git to handle various file types and ensure consistency across different environments."}]
